title: Going home
hookLine: at Sikh funerals the bedtime prayer Kirtan Sohila is sung, and death is spoken of as going home (Guru Granth Sahib 12–13)

lines: THE SAME HYMNS AT A CREMATION.
cards: Night, in a Sikh home. The lights are low, the day's noise is over, and before sleep someone reads a short set of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib. They're called Kirtan Sohila, and they're meant for the end of the day.
Now a different scene: a cremation. The family has gathered, the fire has been lit, and the same hymns are sung. The words that close an ordinary evening also close a life.
Some readers hear in that a single thought: sleep and death are both a kind of going home.

teach.b: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, names Kirtan Sohila as the prayer to recite before sleeping.

It also says that at a cremation, once the pyre is lit, Kirtan Sohila is recited and the Ardas, the Sikh prayer of petition, is offered. The first hymn, by Guru Nanak, doesn't sound like a funeral at all.
The soul is pictured as a bride whose wedding date has already been written. Her friends are told to gather, to pour oil on the threshold, a wedding custom, and to bless her so she may meet her Lord.
In this picture, death isn't a thief at the door. It's the groom's party arriving.
The hymn goes on: the call goes out to every home, every day. Remember the One who calls. The day is coming.

It's said gently, the way a mother reminds a child that the bus will come in the morning. Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul returning to the One it came from, and of accepting it as God's will.
The Rehat Maryada asks mourners not to wail or beat their breasts, but to turn to the hymns.
Grief isn't forbidden; it's given a song.
Some readers hear the nightly singing as a small rehearsal for the night that ends everything, and the singing at a cremation as tucking someone in.

how: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep each night, and at a cremation it is recited after the pyre is lit, followed by the Ardas; mourners are asked to sing hymns rather than wail.

games.q: you're choosing words to sing as a loved one's pyre is lit. what does the Sikh code of conduct name?
games.why: the same hymns that close each night are recited at the cremation, then the Ardas is offered.

practice: Hum something quietly, any gentle tune you know well, a lullaby, a hymn, a song from home, low and soft, barely more than breath, and feel it in the chest and the face.
Let it be the sound of a day closing, a door shut gently for the night. If you know a line of Sohila, or a prayer of your own tradition, you can hum or say that instead.

wordCard.voice: Going home: how the Sikh bedtime hymns, Kirtan Sohila, sung each night and at cremations, picture death: a bride's wedding, a call to every home, a soul returning. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, from the Guru Granth Sahib: the Sikh bedtime hymns, also sung at cremations.

carryVoice: Your line: tucking someone in. The same song closes a day and a life. Sleep well tonight.
